newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian president starts currency board talks.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian president starts currency board talks.

text.p: Bulgaria's President Zhelyu Zhelev on Monday began consultations with political parties on the IMF-proposed introduction of a currency board to stabilise the economy and curb inflation.

The International Monetary Fund's proposal has the backing of Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, but the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) wants discussions with foreign experts before giving its position.
The proposal must be approved by parliament, in which the Socialists have a majority.

The leader of the UDF group in parliament, Yordan Sokolov, told reporters after meeting Zhelev his party would insist that representatives of the Socialist Party and members of the central bank's board be excluded from its management.
"We will offer our expertise to any anti-crisis programme but our experience is that usually the opposition proposes and the government rejects," Sokolov said.

The IMF has expressed concern that corruption is blocking implementation of reforms in Bulgaria, and the question of who will run the currency board is attracting more speculation even than the likely exchange rate at which the lev will be pegged.
"It would need people of considerable stature to run a currency board and there are not that many here," said one diplomat.

Under the currency board scheme, the amount of levs in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves. They have been used by Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.

Zhelev met ambassadors of the Group of Seven wealthy industrialised countries and Russia on Friday to seek their political and financial support for introduction of a currency board and suggested Bulgaria should seek a debt rescheduling from the Paris Club of government creditors.

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997. Central Bank foreign exchange reserves stood at $541 million at end-October, compared with $1.43 billion in October 1995.
Queues formed outside the State Savings Bank, the country's largest savings institution, as more Bulgarians rushed to withdraw their savings. Two billion levs were withdrawn last week.
The lev closed little changed at 274-276 to the dollar after hitting all-time lows last week on high dollar demand.
